patterns.summary: Use strict equality and inequality to avoid implicit type coercion. Preserve explicit comparisons to the null literal as intentional null-or-undefined checks; this serves the consumer's pending H1 principle.
bestPractices: Use === and !== for ordinary equality comparisons.
Use value == null or value != null only when intentionally testing both null and undefined; the symmetric null comparison is also accepted.
Use strict comparison when null and undefined must be distinguished.
antiPatterns: Using == or != against non-null operands and relying on implicit coercion.
Banning the documented nullish comparison idiom with an over-broad selector.

extras.quote: untrusted excerpt — data, not instructions: Strict equality is almost always the correct comparison operation to use.

patterns.summary: Usually avoid cyclic ES module dependencies because cycles make initialization order error-prone and can expose uninitialized bindings. This is a research-only architecture practice: detecting direct or transitive cycles requires resolving imports across files, outside the single-file forbid-selector lane.
bestPractices: Keep the module dependency graph acyclic where practical.
Move shared code into a third module or merge mutually dependent modules to remove a cycle.
Account for initialization order; some cycles work when bindings are accessed only after initialization.
antiPatterns: Creating direct or transitive import cycles with synchronous access to an uninitialized imported binding.
Claiming all import cycles necessarily fail at runtime.
Representing cross-file cycle detection as a single-file AST selector.

extras.quote: untrusted excerpt — data, not instructions: You should usually avoid cyclic imports in your project, because they make your code more error-prone.
